description: I am an architecture student, and my teammate is a law graduate. I am interested in animation, science fiction, space architecture, biology, and animal habitats. My skills include 2D/3D modeling, illustration, video editing, game design, and creative writing. My teammate specializes in research, data analysis, app development, and problem-solving. Together, we combine different perspectives to create original and innovative ideas.
summary:
Bio-Inspired Mars Habitat Game

Our project argues that the first life on Mars should follow humanity’s own path: learning from nature. Just as early humans observed animals and turned those observations into science and technology, our educational game applies the same logic to Mars.

The first challenge on Mars is survival and efficient resource management, which begins with choosing the habitat best suited to Martian conditions. Players select habitats inspired by animal burrows and nests, each integrating its natural model’s engineering solutions: passive thermal regulation, structural load distribution, ventilation, humidity control, and radiation shielding through subsurface or regolith-covered volumes.

Each habitat also shapes resource management. Energy, water, oxygen, and materials are allocated according to the habitat’s geometry, thermal performance, and spatial organization, showing how design decisions drive efficiency and sustainability.

The game builds children’s awareness of science, technology, and nature. After playing, a child watching an ant colony may recognize an underground city and ask how its inhabitants meet their needs and manage resources.
details:
Project Name: Neighbors of DEIMOS

What does it do and how does it work?
Neighbors of Deimos is a browser-based Mars mission trainer for ages 7–12. The player is the only astronaut and must survive 14 sols. Before landing, the player chooses cargo within a limited budget: solar panels, a wind turbine, batteries, packaged food, oxygen, water, spare parts, extra shielding and pre-grown seedlings. The player then picks one of five habitats inspired by animal nests (ant colony, rufous hornero, caddisfly larva, honeybee comb and cave swallow) and a landing site. On each sol the player makes decisions under radiation, dust, temperature, carbon dioxide and water pressure. Every nest solves one problem and creates another, so no habitat is best at everything. For example, digging deep like ants gives radiation shielding but costs energy, and building with soil like the hornero uses abundant material but takes time. Each run uses a mission seed that is shown on the result screen, so a run can be repeated and compared.

What are the benefits?
Children practice systems thinking: every engineering choice has a resource cost. Simplified terms such as sol and radiation are explained in plain language inside the game. It runs in a browser with no download and no account, and it plays offline.

What is the intended impact?
Early humans learned from animals, and that observation grew into science and technology. The game shows the same path for the first life on Mars. After playing, a child watching ants may ask how an underground city is organized, how its inhabitants meet their needs and how they manage their resources. We aim to turn a Mars habitat decision into curiosity about nature and engineering.

Tools, languages, hardware and software used

  • A single HTML/CSS/JavaScript file with no backend. Resource calculations are pure, testable functions, kept separate from the drawing code.
    • Perseverance MEDA, for Mars surface temperature and other environmental measurements
    • Curiosity RAD, for surface radiation, including the May 2024 solar storm
    • DONKI, for space-weather events
    • NASA’s Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, for oxygen, water and food consumption
  • CSA youth and food-production resources
  • Original hand-drawn characters and illustrations by our team. Visuals drawn in code with AI assistance are labeled in the game.
  • AI-assisted development (Claude, Chatgpt, rendair ai), stage by stage from a prompt series we designed

How creative is the project?
Biomimicry is the central game mechanic. The habitat options are real animal nests, and each one changes how energy, shielding, time and materials trade off. The game also uses one visual identity, our own hand drawings, and connects Mars engineering to what a child sees in an ant colony.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific integrity: nothing is made up, archive data is labeled as archive, and unavailable data is stated as unavailable. Only solar storms verified to have affected Mars are used.
  • Honesty about the model: game numbers are simplified educational values, and the game says so. It is not presented as a NASA-approved simulator.
  • Physical realism: seedlings arrive already grown, because seeds sown on Mars would not mature within 14 sols.
  • Age-appropriate language and design for 7–12, with touch and keyboard support
  • Challenge rules: we separated required items from suggested resources, and we use no NASA logos or insignia.
